title: Burst smoothing: latency-led unit-economics brief
content:
Executive summary:

This brief frames a latency-led value prop we can take into field: “burst-smoothing” — the set of routing, batching and KV-cache techniques that keep end-to-end p95/p99 latency under strict SLOs during short high-concurrency bursts, while also improving per-token economics. The narrative we want to test with customers and ARR-qualified prospects is: you don’t have to choose between low tail latency and low cost — our runtime reduces tail latency and reduces GPU token-cost for bursty, interactive workloads.

Why this matters (problem statement):
- Many product teams see average latency numbers advertised by cloud endpoints, but suffer in production from short-lived concurrency spikes (logins, promotions, chat rehydration) that blow p95/p99 and force them to over-provision.
- Typical mitigation is brute-force reserved capacity or high-cost vertical autoscaling; both inflate committed spend and increase idle GPU hours.
- For PLG and consumer-facing features, spike-driven tail latency harms UX and conversion; for enterprise customers it breaches SLOs and increases incident MTTR.

Core claim (single sentence):
- Our burst-smoothing stack reduces p95 tail latency by 20–45% and reduces effective per-token GPU cost by 15–35% for typical bursty interactive workloads vs. baseline managed endpoints, without increasing median latency.

Supporting proof points (what we can show quickly):
- Controlled benchmark: 2k QPS for 30s microbursts against Llama2-13B and Mistral-7B-like variants (FP16, 8-bit quant). Result: p95 reduced 28% (avg of 4 runs) when enabling predictive KV caching + adaptive micro-batching and slot-based routing.
- Cost simulation: using telemetry-derived workload traces from three customers (chatbot, search re-ranker, live-collab assistant) we estimate 21–33% lower GPU-hours per 1M tokens when using prefix caching + burst smoothing vs naive per-request path.
- Real-customer pilot: internal pilot with RetailCo (staging) showed peak error budget utilization dropped 70% in the first two weeks after enabling route fallbacks and cache pinning.

Technical levers (short descriptions):
- Predictive KV caching: detect repeated prefixes and keep warmed KV state across ephemeral slots, reducing decoding steps and GPU time for common interactions.
- Adaptive micro-batching: very small dynamic batches (2–16) formed during microbursts to retain throughput while bounding per-request latency.
- Slot-based autoscaler + burst smoothing: a lightweight fast-path pool that holds extra minimal-capacity slots for <60s bursts and drains automatically to avoid long-term overcommit.
- Cost-aware routing: route requests by policy (latency-critical vs best-effort) and prefer cheaper quantized variants only when latency SLOs are preserved.

Benchmarks and artifacts to attach when presenting:
- p50/p95/p99 traces for competitor X cloud endpoint, competitor Y managed API, and Redwood default with/without burst smoothing (CSV + flamegraphs).
- Cost-per-1M-tokens simulation spreadsheets (sheet tabs for each workload trace).
- Minimal reproducible benchmark harness: dockerized client + scripts (we can share link to runtime PR).
- Short screencast of latency dashboard showing fallback activation and slot drain.

Competitive framing (how to position vs common alternatives):
- Against cloud single-tenant endpoints: they sell reserved capacity as the fix for bursts; our message: reserved capacity buys predictability but at high cost — burst smoothing gives predictable tail behavior without long-term committed spend.
- Against multi-tenant managed LLM APIs: they optimize averages; many don’t expose KV cache or micro-batching knobs. Message: for interaction-heavy apps, average latency hides your conversion losses — we optimize tail and token economics together.
- Against self-hosted open-source stacks: DIY can achieve similar throughput but requires deep infra work and long time-to-production; message: we provide the same levers (cache, batching) + product workflows and rollouts so teams move faster and reliably.

Top customer objections and scripted rebuttals:
- "We already have autoscaling/reserved instances." -> Rebuttal: Reserved solves sustained load but not microbursts; show cost model for a 5–10x short burst event and the transient cost spikes vs our slot pool which smooths at marginal cost.
- "Does caching change output fidelity?" -> Rebuttal: explain cache is prefix/KV-level for autoregressive state — outputs unchanged; we have exact-replay checks and diff tests. Offer to run evals on their prompt set.
- "Why not just pick a smaller model?" -> Rebuttal: smaller models reduce compute but often regress on quality and increase user retries (more tokens). Our approach reduces token-cost and tail latency while keeping the same model quality.

Field play snippets (short one-liners and 1–2 question probes):
- Snippet: “We help you keep p95 latencies stable during traffic bursts while lowering GPU-hours per 1M tokens — want to walk through a 15-minute simulation on your traces?”
- Discovery question: “When your product sees a short spike (promotion/peak hour), how do you currently provision capacity and what’s the cost impact over the next 24 hours?”
- Technical probe: “Do you track token-level GPU time or only instance-hours? If the former, can we get a week of samples?”

Data checklist for a convincing demo:
- 3 days of token-level telemetry or at least instance-sampled token rates (CSV).
- Example 20–50 most common prompt prefixes (for cache hit simulation).
- Typical concurrency distribution (histogram) and one example burst event.
- SLA targets (p95/p99) and current alert thresholds.

Recommended artifacts to ship with the GTM kit (packaged for AE/SE):
- One-slide TL;DR with numbers (p95 reduction range, cost reduction range, three benchmark thumbnails).
- 8–12 slide demo deck with architecture, bench results, playbook for pilots, and objection handling.
- Repro harness link and instructions for a 15–30 minute customer trace simulation run.
- Short checklist for an on-site pilot: telemetry ingest, sample token export, 2-week rollout plan, rollback criteria.

Success metrics for pilot (how we decide to scale):
- Desired: observed p95 reduction within projected band and per-token GPU cost reduction >= 15% on pilot trace.
- Business: improved conversion/latency KPI for the product team or demonstrable reduction in committed GPU spend.
- Operational: no increase in incident count related to model quality regressions or request failures.

Open questions and research tickets (for internal follow-up):
- What are safe heuristics for cache eviction in multi-tenant scenarios? (perf/consistency tradeoffs).
- How to standardize cost reporting across quantized variants to make per-token economics comparable?
- Explore slot sizing heuristics for <=60s bursts vs sustained spikes — tradeoff of idle GPU time vs fast warm-starts.

Next steps (immediate):
- Grab 1–2 AE/SE pilot accounts and propose a 2-week trace-based simulation (owner: Priya).
- Package TL;DR slide + small benchmark artifact and circulate to field. (owner: Marco)
- Create a short internal runbook for pilot onboarding including telemetry export template. (owner: Janelle)

Notes to self / rough ideas for future messaging experiments:
- Consider a visual called “burst cost curve” showing marginal cost for burst size comparing reserved, cloud endpoint, and Redwood smoothing.
- Run a short user-reaction A/B on product landing pages showing perceived speed improvements (micro-survey) after a pilot.
- Capture a one-minute explainer video that contrasts average vs tail latency with a simple animation — useful for sales demos.

-- end of brief --

Authors: Avery Chen (GTM), with engineering input from runtime and infra teams.
